claims.target_lexeme: skedaddle, v. (< Northern British scaddle / skaddle + expressive -addle)
claims.short_label: Northern British/Scots-Irish scaddle/skaddle ('bolt in fright') + expressive -addle derivation hypothesis
claims.statement: Pre-1859 Northern English and Scots-border dialectal scaddle / SKADDLE ('skittish, wild, spoken of young horses that fly out; to scare, run off in a fright'—verified in Ray 1691, Grose 1787 'North.', Carr Craven 1828 SKADDLE beside SKALE 'disperse', Brockett 1846, and Wright EDD 1904/1905), reinforced by Scots skail ('disperse under terror', Jamieson 1808) and expressive American gait/motion verbs in -addle (straddle, waddle, paddle, scuddle/scuttle, Webster 1828), provides the strongest phonological and semantic pathway to American intransitive skedaddle (/skɪˈdæd.əl/).
claims.rationale: Unlike post-1862 transitive milk-spilling glosses or impossible Greek/Swedish/Gaelic etymologies, Northern British scaddle/skaddle is primary-scan verified from 1691–1846 in the exact intransitive 'bolt/run off in fright' semantic field and requires only standard American unstressed-prefix/expressive frequentative remodeling (Liberman 2008).

evidence_boundary.establishes: Continuous 1691–1846 Northern English and Scots-border print attestation of scaddle/skaddle ('bolt, run off in fright') and Scots skail ('disperse in terror'), plus pre-1859 English availability of scuddle/scuttle and -addle motion templates.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Direct pre-1859 American print attestation of an intermediate trisyllabic bridge spelling (*scadaddle / *skaddle -> skedaddle) catching the morphological expansion in progress.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Exact decade and regional American speech community (Midland/Scots-Irish vs. Upstate New York/Western Reserve) in which disyllabic scaddle/skaddle expanded to iambic-amphibrachic skedaddle.

limitations: Remains an inferential morphological reconstruction because no pre-1859 American text preserves an explicit metalinguistic bridge between regional 'scaddle/skaddle' and trisyllabic 'skedaddle'.
resolution_criteria: Locate pre-1859 American frontier manuscripts, county newspapers, or regional glossaries attesting disyllabic 'scaddle'/'skaddle' ('bolt, run off') or transitional spellings alongside 'skedaddle'.

evidence.reason: Attests 'Scaddle; To scare, or fright' and 'Scaddle, wild, mischievous, spoken of young horses that fly out' in John Ray's 1691 Collection of English Words (2nd ed., p. 159; absent in 1674 1st ed.).
Reclassifies 'SCADDLE' explicitly as Northern English ('North.') in Francis Grose's 1787 Provincial Glossary.
Attests Scots 'To SKAIL, SKALE' ('to disperse, scatter under the impression of terror') in Jamieson's 1808 Dictionary (and 1825 Supplement 'SCAWPATE').
Attests Northern English <sk-> spelling 'SKADDLE' ('wild, mischievous, frightening') alongside 'SKALE' ('disperse') in William Carr's 1828 Yorkshire Craven Glossary.
Attests Newcastle/Northumbrian 'SCADDLE, skittish, wild' in John Trotter Brockett's 1846 Glossary of North Country Words (3rd ed.).
Verifies pre-1859 American speed/gait templates SCUD, SCUDDLE, SCUTTLE ('run with affected precipitation'), and STRADDLE in Noah Webster's 1828 American Dictionary.
Documents regional British 'SCADDLE, v. To run off in a fright' (p. 233) alongside 'SKEDADDLE' in Wright's English Dialect Dictionary (1904/1905).
Synthesizes Anatoly Liberman's (2008) phonological analysis of expressive /sk-/ + '-addle' expansion from scaddle/skaddle.
Anchors the target American intransitive motion sense ('skedaddled for home') in June 1859 frontier speech.
Separates pre-1859 documented scaddle/skaddle ('bolt in fright') from post-1862 British transitive 'spill milk' testimonies.

claims.target_lexeme: skedaddle, v. (alleged Ancient Greek σκεδάννυμι derivation)
claims.short_label: Rebuttal of the Civil War Harvard / Ancient Greek σκεδάννυμι (skedannymi) folk etymology
claims.statement: The popular 1861–1864 journalistic and dictionary derivation of skedaddle from Ancient Greek σκεδάννυμι (skedannymi, aorist ἐσκέδασα, 'scatter, disperse'—promoted in May–October 1862 press columns and copied into Hotten's 1864 Slang Dictionary before Hotten deleted it in 1874) is refuted on morphological and chronological grounds: Greek -άννυμι / -άσω has no regular or slang pathway to English -addle, and the earliest 1859–1861 witnesses belong to Missouri–Platte–Kansas frontier vernacular rather than Harvard or Army of the Potomac classical wit.
claims.rationale: Primary scans of Liddell & Scott (1851) and the 1862–1874 press/Hotten chain prove the Greek comparison was a facetious post-hoc Civil War pun invented after skedaddle reached Eastern newspapers in late 1861.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Morphological, register, and textual-genealogy refutation of deriving skedaddle from Ancient Greek σκεδάννυμι, including Hotten's own 1874 retraction.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absence of secondary humorous awareness of Greek σκεδάννυμι among college-educated Eastern journalists in 1862.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None; closed on morphological and 1859 frontier-chronology grounds.

limitations: CERT-2600-207 and CERT-2600-312 inspect Hotten's 1864/1874 Slang Dictionary editions, where the 1864 paragraph was lifted verbatim from the October 1862 London Spectator (CERT-2600-205).

evidence.reason: Verifies Greek stem morphology (σκεδάννυμι, fut. σκεδάσω) in Liddell & Scott (1851, p. 1344) and documents Hotten's 1874 deletion of his 1864 Greek etymology.
Documents the May–June 1862 Historical Magazine antiquarian notes proposing Greek σκεδάννυμι.
Documents the August 2, 1862 Philadelphia Press embellishment attributing the Greek pun to a 'Harvard professor'.
Supplies the October 1862 London Spectator critique mocking Lord Hill via Greek skedannumi.
Exposes Hotten's 1864 'Greek' entry as an uncredited verbatim copy of the October 1862 Spectator column.
Proves skedaddle circulated in low-register June 1859 Pike's Peak overland verse two years before Eastern wartime classical puns.

claims.short_label: Rebuttal of the 1864 Webster / 1872 Schele De Vere Swedish and Danish ghost-word etymology
claims.statement: The 1864 Webster Dictionary claim of Scandinavian immigrant origin in the Upper Midwest and Maximilian Schele De Vere's (1872) cited Swedish '*skuddadahl' and Danish '*skyededehl' are refuted by primary Scandinavian dictionaries: Carl Deleen's Swedish and English Pocket-Dictionary (1829, p. 413) records only skudda ('to shake off' dust, Matt. 10:14) and Ferrall & Repp's Danish-English Dictionary (1845, p. 288) records only skudde sig ('shrug, shake oneself'), proving '*skuddadahl' and '*skyededehl' are non-existent ghost words.
claims.rationale: Direct inspection of pre-1859 Swedish and Danish lexicons confirms OED1's 1911 skepticism: neither language possesses a '-dahl/-dehl' compound verb meaning 'flee', and Swedish palatalizes sk- before front vowels rather than preserving English [skɪ-].

evidence_boundary.establishes: Lexicographical proof that Schele De Vere's '*skuddadahl' and '*skyededehl' are fabricated ghost words and that Swedish skudda / Danish skudde mean 'shake/shrug' rather than 'run away'.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Positive etymological origin outside refuting the Scandinavian hypothesis.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None; closed by primary Swedish (1829) and Danish (1845) dictionary verification.

limitations: Evaluates standard and colloquial 19th-century Swedish and Danish lexical inventories cited by Webster (1864) and Schele De Vere (1872).

evidence.reason: Verifies in Deleen (1829, p. 413) and Ferrall & Repp (1845, p. 288) that '*skuddadahl' and '*skyededehl' do not exist and skudda/skudde mean 'shake off / shrug'.
Documents Schele De Vere's 1872 Americanisms (pp. 634–635) printing the spurious forms 'skuddadahl' and 'skyededehl'.
Records W. A. Craigie's OED1 note (1911) rejecting the alleged Swedish/Danish words as lacking any evidence of existence.

claims.target_lexeme: skedaddle, v. (alleged Irish/Scottish Gaelic sgaoil, sgudal, and *sgedad ol derivations)
claims.short_label: Rebuttal of Irish/Scottish Gaelic sgaoil, sgudal, sgath+adhl, and ghost '*sgedad ol' etymologies
claims.statement: Nineteenth-century Celtic derivations of skedaddle—from Irish/Gaelic sgaoil ('scatter'), Scottish Gaelic sgudal, Charles Mackay's (1877) arbitrary segmentation sgath + adhl, and the December 1862 Historical Magazine claim that the Irish New Testament prints '*sgedad ol' at Matthew 26:31—are refuted by primary Gaelic lexicons and biblical texts: sgaoil/scaoil is monosyllabic [sˠkiːlʲ] lacking dental stops -d-dd-, sgudal means 'fish-guts, offal' (Macbain 1896), and the 1602 Irish New Testament actually reads 'scaoilfidhear tréd na gcaorach' with zero trace of '*sgedad ol'.
claims.rationale: Checking O'Reilly (1817), Macbain (1896), and William Daniel's 1602 Tiomna Nuadh exposes '*sgedad ol' (repeated uncritically by Schele De Vere 1872 and Bartlett 1877) as a fabricated biblical ghost quotation.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Phonological, semantic, and textual falsification of Irish/Scottish Gaelic sgaoil, sgudal, sgath + adhl, and the spurious Matthew 26:31 '*sgedad ol' quotation.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absence of Scots-Irish English dialect speakers (speaking Northern British/Ulster Scots English rather than Gaelic) in transmitting scaddle/skaddle.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None; '*sgedad ol' is directly falsified against the Irish New Testament text of Matthew 26:31.

limitations: Separates Gaelic-language etymons (refuted here) from English-language Scots/Ulster-Scots dialectal scaddle/skaddle (evaluated in CLM-2600-011).

evidence.reason: Verifies O'Reilly (1817, Sgaoil [sˠkiːlʲ]), Macbain (1896, sgudal 'fish-guts, offal'), Mackay's baseless 1877 sgath+adhl conjecture, and the 1602 Irish NT reading at Matt. 26:31.
Identifies the December 1862 Historical Magazine correspondent 'B. H. H.' who introduced the spurious Irish Testament '*sgedad ol' claim.
Documents Schele De Vere (1872) propagating the false '*sgedad ol' Irish Testament claim.
Documents Bartlett (1877) repeating Irish 'sgaoil' from the 1862–1872 press literature.
